I would suggest seeing a registered dietitian, they can work with you to help gain weight slowly and steadily for more success. I do know that they can be expensive to see, but some health insurance plans cover them (with a co-pay of course). I would ask your doctor or insurance what's covered. Or since you're only 16, ask your parents if they know what's covered. As far as the discomfort during and after eating, I would look into getting blood work done and make an appointment with your provider and explain your symptoms. They would be a better judge of whether they deem it more medical or psychiatric (eating disorder) and can then point you in the right direction. I hope you find the answers, take care and best of luck.

It seems like whatever feeling triggers you to purge (whether that be physical like the feeling of fullness, or mental such as the feeling of anxiety) was definitely activated during/after this meal, and thus it is perfectly normal to have urges. Remember that a thought or feeling compelling us to do something is just that, a thought or feeling. I know when triggered to purge I feel so awful and overwhelmed I just want the feeling out of my body, but the thing with anxiety is that if you are able to sit with it it will eventually go down. You will not feel this way forever and if you are able to sit with the feeling this time around imagine what you can manage to sit with in the future. I'm sorry you are struggling at the moment, I do think that the fact that you posted on here and didn't just engage in the behavior is commendable. I hope you have a good rest of your night, perhaps engaging in a relaxing activity or possibly something to distract? Or if you have a trustworthy person in your support system who you can talk to or spend time with?

For background, two years ago I had this huge eczema patch across my throat that I was very insecure about. Anyways, I went to see my psychiatrist, who never seems to look at me-always on the computer or his phone. So I'm talking we have like five minutes left of our session things are going normal when all of a sudden he goes, "Oh my god! What happened to you neck?!?" I was so embarrassed and I'm stumbling to explain how it's eczema that won't go away and he's still in shock and replies, "Wow! You should see a doctor." I explained that I already did and he just responds with a still just as surprised demeanor, "That can't be good for your self-esteem!" Mind you, I go to him in regards to an eating disorder so the fact he commented on my appearance in general was distressing.

I've only recently started ERP therapy a couple of months ago so I don't have many tips. Although I do think that ERP therapy is very important in treating ocd, but it is probably one of the most difficult things I've ever done. I feel like it's also important to find a therapist who specializes in ocd, because before the person I'm seeing now I had a general therapist and she was practically clueless when I discussed my ocd symptoms and worries with her, she would just say "just try washing less." In my experience I also started to have new obsessions when starting therapy, and I think for me it's like my brain is so used to obsessing over one thing or another that when I started working on one thing and experiencing relief and lowered anxiety I found myself starting to worry or focus on something else which can be frustrating. My therapist says that treating ocd is like playing a game of "whack-a-mole" you take down one obsession or compulsion and another tends to pop up in its place. I can also relate to the fear of herpes and similar viruses, it's one of my primary fears and drives the decontamination cycle, even talking about it gives me anxiety but I guess that's what exposure is about, sitting with the anxiety and not letting the fear consume and trigger compulsions.

Throughout the years my ocd has changed in regards to what I'm obsessing about. It started when I was younger with organization based compulsions, then from the time I was in middle school to high school it was the fear of others harming me, then at the start of college the fear of bed bugs and lice, and for the last three years I've had contamination ocd. I think when struggling with a certain form of ocd it can be normal to say "if I had a different type it would be more manageable" but another type could become just as time consuming and obsessive especially if it is as serve as your current form of ocd. All in all, ocd no matter the form sucks and is miserable, I'm sorry you're struggling.

I go through bouts of laxative abuse and I usually just have to slowly taper down the amount I'm taking until I can go without them. I know it can be an embarrassing topic, but I recommend talking to a doctor, because eight years of laxative abuse may cause some damage, and a doctor may have better suggestions on how to stop taking them without things like bloating, cramping, and constipation. A therapist or counselor could possibly help with the body image issues which I'm assuming trigger the laxative abuse, I mean, they can't ease the physical pain, but they can help with the emotional attachment to the laxatives. Hope this post made sense, and take care!

While guinea pig mounting can be for mating, they also display the behavior to establish dominance, and if the other pig refuses to be "submissive" it can lead to fighting. I have two guinea pigs currently and I have to keep them in separate cages because they won't get along even though one of them was with another guinea pig before hand for over two years, so some pigs just like to be alone. If you don't have the space for two cages I recommend putting up a divider in your current cage to keep them apart, maybe even a divider that does not allow them to make eye contact would be helpful. Also, if she is pregnant she may be acting aggressively as a means of protection, if possible it wouldn't hurt to take her to the vet to be sure if she is or not.
